method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from Clinical Oncology Society of Australia (COSA) 'Medications to lower the risk of breast cancer: clinician guide' (Version 7, approved by COSA Council 22 March 2024), 23 claims; LICENCE: COSA website terms: personal, non-commercial use only; 'Any other use is strictly prohibited.' (the PDF itself carries no licence statement) (read at https://www.cosa.org.au/common/Uploaded%20files/Policies/003_website-terms-and-conditions-of-use_v004_approved_5august2022.pdf). S2: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), UK 'Familial breast cancer: classification, care and managing breast cancer and related risks in people with a family history of breast cancer (CG164), Recommendations' (published 25 June 2013, last updated 14 November 2023), 7 claims; LICENCE: © NICE. NICE 'Notice of Rights': reuse under the NICE UK Open Content Licence in the UK only; outside the UK, no reproduction without NICE's prior written agreement (read at https://www.nice.org.uk/terms-and-conditions (section 18, Notice of Rights)). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 keeps every COSA claim (S1) unchanged and adds S2, NICE CG164 (the UK national guideline, last updated 2023), for risk category thresholds and a ranked choice of medicine by menopausal status and risk level. S2 is paraphrased and hash-anchored; NICE's words are not reproduced. NICE's AI-use clause, recorded verbatim per the standing owner decision: 'Copyright content owned by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) may be made available to individuals and commercial/non-commercial organisations on a non-exclusive basis for artificial intelligence (AI) purposes. All requests, without exception, are subject to an approval process, licensing arrangement and a fee (for international use).' The ASCO 2019 risk-reduction guideline (J Clin Oncol) and the ESMO 2023 hereditary breast-ovarian guideline (Annals of Oncology) are not open on Europe PMC. Only the Recommendations chapter was used; the risk-category table under 'Terms used in this guideline' was not used.

claims.claim: **Offer a risk-reducing medicine to high-risk women who decline or delay risk-reducing mastectomy, and to women with raised risk that does not justify surgery.** Do not offer it at population risk, where harms probably outweigh benefits. Never continue it beyond 5 years.
claims.locator: Clinical Oncology Society of Australia (COSA), 'Medications to lower the risk of breast cancer: clinician guide', Version 7, approved by COSA Council 22 March 2024, https://www.cosa.org.au/common/Uploaded%20files/Guidelines/breast-ca-risk-reducing-meds_clinician-guide_22032024.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Measure absolute risk formally first**, so the absolute benefit can be set against the absolute chance of harm. iPrevent (Tyrer-Cuzick and BOADICEA/CanRisk) gives these estimates for each SERM.
claims.locator: Clinical Oncology Society of Australia (COSA), 'Medications to lower the risk of breast cancer: clinician guide', Version 7, approved by COSA Council 22 March 2024, https://www.cosa.org.au/common/Uploaded%20files/Guidelines/breast-ca-risk-reducing-meds_clinician-guide_22032024.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Keep up screening suited to her age and risk**, and discuss medicines alongside lifestyle change (hormone use, alcohol, body weight, exercise, breastfeeding) and, where risk is high, bilateral risk-reducing mastectomy.
claims.locator: Clinical Oncology Society of Australia (COSA), 'Medications to lower the risk of breast cancer: clinician guide', Version 7, approved by COSA Council 22 March 2024, https://www.cosa.org.au/common/Uploaded%20files/Guidelines/breast-ca-risk-reducing-meds_clinician-guide_22032024.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **What to tell her about the limits:** all four medicines lower only oestrogen-receptor-positive cancer, and none has been shown to reduce breast cancer deaths or deaths from any cause.
claims.locator: Clinical Oncology Society of Australia (COSA), 'Medications to lower the risk of breast cancer: clinician guide', Version 7, approved by COSA Council 22 March 2024, https://www.cosa.org.au/common/Uploaded%20files/Guidelines/breast-ca-risk-reducing-meds_clinician-guide_22032024.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Before menopause, tamoxifen is the only option.** After menopause, tamoxifen, raloxifene, exemestane and anastrozole all work.
claims.locator: Clinical Oncology Society of Australia (COSA), 'Medications to lower the risk of breast cancer: clinician guide', Version 7, approved by COSA Council 22 March 2024, https://www.cosa.org.au/common/Uploaded%20files/Guidelines/breast-ca-risk-reducing-meds_clinician-guide_22032024.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Tamoxifen 20 mg daily for 5 years** cuts relative risk by at least a third, before or after menopause, and the protection lasts at least 20 years.
claims.locator: Clinical Oncology Society of Australia (COSA), 'Medications to lower the risk of breast cancer: clinician guide', Version 7, approved by COSA Council 22 March 2024, https://www.cosa.org.au/common/Uploaded%20files/Guidelines/breast-ca-risk-reducing-meds_clinician-guide_22032024.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Low-dose tamoxifen, 5 mg daily for 3 years**, also lowers risk by one third or more, lasting 10 years or longer, with significantly fewer hot flushes. It has not been tested head-to-head against 20 mg, so use it for women who cannot tolerate the standard dose.
claims.locator: Clinical Oncology Society of Australia (COSA), 'Medications to lower the risk of breast cancer: clinician guide', Version 7, approved by COSA Council 22 March 2024, https://www.cosa.org.au/common/Uploaded%20files/Guidelines/breast-ca-risk-reducing-meds_clinician-guide_22032024.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **There is no 5 mg tablet.** Prescribe 10 mg every second day on a private script (the 10 mg strength is not PBS-subsidised for prevention); tamoxifen's long half-life makes this reasonable.
claims.locator: Clinical Oncology Society of Australia (COSA), 'Medications to lower the risk of breast cancer: clinician guide', Version 7, approved by COSA Council 22 March 2024, https://www.cosa.org.au/common/Uploaded%20files/Guidelines/breast-ca-risk-reducing-meds_clinician-guide_22032024.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Raloxifene 60 mg daily for five years** (post-menopausal women only) matches tamoxifen early on but is less effective in the longer term. It carries no endometrial cancer risk and causes fewer cataracts.
claims.locator: Clinical Oncology Society of Australia (COSA), 'Medications to lower the risk of breast cancer: clinician guide', Version 7, approved by COSA Council 22 March 2024, https://www.cosa.org.au/common/Uploaded%20files/Guidelines/breast-ca-risk-reducing-meds_clinician-guide_22032024.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Anastrozole 1 mg daily for five years** lowers relative risk by 49% over 10 years in post-menopausal women.
claims.locator: Clinical Oncology Society of Australia (COSA), 'Medications to lower the risk of breast cancer: clinician guide', Version 7, approved by COSA Council 22 March 2024, https://www.cosa.org.au/common/Uploaded%20files/Guidelines/breast-ca-risk-reducing-meds_clinician-guide_22032024.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Exemestane 25 mg daily for five years** lowered relative risk by 63% in the short term; longer-term efficacy is unknown. Neither aromatase inhibitor has been compared with the other or with a SERM.
claims.locator: Clinical Oncology Society of Australia (COSA), 'Medications to lower the risk of breast cancer: clinician guide', Version 7, approved by COSA Council 22 March 2024, https://www.cosa.org.au/common/Uploaded%20files/Guidelines/breast-ca-risk-reducing-meds_clinician-guide_22032024.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Tamoxifen and raloxifene raise the risk of DVT and PE:** on average about 1 extra case in 250 women over 5 years on tamoxifen and 1 in 330 on raloxifene, lower before menopause. Teach women the symptoms.
claims.locator: Clinical Oncology Society of Australia (COSA), 'Medications to lower the risk of breast cancer: clinician guide', Version 7, approved by COSA Council 22 March 2024, https://www.cosa.org.au/common/Uploaded%20files/Guidelines/breast-ca-risk-reducing-meds_clinician-guide_22032024.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Tamoxifen raises endometrial cancer risk after menopause only** (about 1 extra case per 250 women over 5 years), and the excess falls away once it stops. Ask women to report any post-menopausal vaginal bleeding promptly.
claims.locator: Clinical Oncology Society of Australia (COSA), 'Medications to lower the risk of breast cancer: clinician guide', Version 7, approved by COSA Council 22 March 2024, https://www.cosa.org.au/common/Uploaded%20files/Guidelines/breast-ca-risk-reducing-meds_clinician-guide_22032024.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Everyday side-effects of tamoxifen:** vasomotor symptoms in about 1 extra woman in 10, and possibly cataract in about 1 extra in 250. It also lightens or disturbs periods without causing menopause.
claims.locator: Clinical Oncology Society of Australia (COSA), 'Medications to lower the risk of breast cancer: clinician guide', Version 7, approved by COSA Council 22 March 2024, https://www.cosa.org.au/common/Uploaded%20files/Guidelines/breast-ca-risk-reducing-meds_clinician-guide_22032024.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Bone:** tamoxifen and raloxifene slow age-related bone loss and cut fracture risk after menopause, whereas the aromatase inhibitors make bone loss worse, so give bone-health advice (calcium, vitamin D, exercise, no smoking).
claims.locator: Clinical Oncology Society of Australia (COSA), 'Medications to lower the risk of breast cancer: clinician guide', Version 7, approved by COSA Council 22 March 2024, https://www.cosa.org.au/common/Uploaded%20files/Guidelines/breast-ca-risk-reducing-meds_clinician-guide_22032024.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **NICE risk categories (from its referral criteria):** moderate risk is a lifetime risk of 17% or more but under 30%, or a 10-year risk at age 40 of more than 3 to 8%; high risk is a lifetime risk of 30% or more, a 10-year risk above 8%, or a 10% or greater chance of a family gene mutation.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), UK, 'Familial breast cancer: classification, care and managing breast cancer and related risks in people with a family history of breast cancer (CG164), Recommendations', published 25 June 2013, last updated 14 November 2023, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg164/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Who discusses it and how:** clinicians in secondary care or specialist genetic clinics talk through absolute benefits and risks with women at high or moderate risk, using a decision aid: the fall in invasive breast cancer, no effect on mortality, side effects, and alternatives such as surveillance alone or, at high risk, risk-reducing surgery.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), UK, 'Familial breast cancer: classification, care and managing breast cancer and related risks in people with a family history of breast cancer (CG164), Recommendations', published 25 June 2013, last updated 14 November 2023, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg164/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **High risk, premenopausal: offer tamoxifen for 5 years,** unless there is a past or raised risk of thromboembolic disease or endometrial cancer.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), UK, 'Familial breast cancer: classification, care and managing breast cancer and related risks in people with a family history of breast cancer (CG164), Recommendations', published 25 June 2013, last updated 14 November 2023, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg164/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **High risk, postmenopausal: NICE puts anastrozole first,** for 5 years, unless osteoporosis is severe. With severe osteoporosis, or if she declines anastrozole: offer tamoxifen for 5 years (if no thromboembolic or endometrial risk), or consider raloxifene for 5 years for a woman with a uterus who has no thromboembolic risk and does not want tamoxifen.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), UK, 'Familial breast cancer: classification, care and managing breast cancer and related risks in people with a family history of breast cancer (CG164), Recommendations', published 25 June 2013, last updated 14 November 2023, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg164/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Moderate risk: the same medicines are 'considered' rather than offered:** tamoxifen for 5 years before menopause; anastrozole for 5 years after menopause unless osteoporosis is severe, with tamoxifen or raloxifene as the alternatives.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), UK, 'Familial breast cancer: classification, care and managing breast cancer and related risks in people with a family history of breast cancer (CG164), Recommendations', published 25 June 2013, last updated 14 November 2023, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg164/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **No chemoprevention after bilateral risk-reducing mastectomy, and none beyond 5 years** in women who have never had breast cancer.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), UK, 'Familial breast cancer: classification, care and managing breast cancer and related risks in people with a family history of breast cancer (CG164), Recommendations', published 25 June 2013, last updated 14 November 2023, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg164/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Stopping tamoxifen (NICE):** a minimum of 2 months ahead of attempting pregnancy, and a minimum of 6 weeks ahead of planned surgery.
claims.locator: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), UK, 'Familial breast cancer: classification, care and managing breast cancer and related risks in people with a family history of breast cancer (CG164), Recommendations', published 25 June 2013, last updated 14 November 2023, https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg164/chapter/Recommendations, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Do not use tamoxifen** when lifetime risk is below 1.5 times population risk, after bilateral mastectomy, after DVT, PE or thrombotic stroke, after endometrial cancer, in smokers, in pregnancy or breastfeeding or when pregnancy is planned within 3 years, with anticoagulants, HRT or the combined pill, or with strong CYP2D6 inhibitors such as some antidepressants.
claims.locator: Clinical Oncology Society of Australia (COSA), 'Medications to lower the risk of breast cancer: clinician guide', Version 7, approved by COSA Council 22 March 2024, https://www.cosa.org.au/common/Uploaded%20files/Guidelines/breast-ca-risk-reducing-meds_clinician-guide_22032024.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Do not use an aromatase inhibitor** before menopause, with HRT, or when bone density testing in the past 2 years showed osteoporosis (take care with osteopenia).
claims.locator: Clinical Oncology Society of Australia (COSA), 'Medications to lower the risk of breast cancer: clinician guide', Version 7, approved by COSA Council 22 March 2024, https://www.cosa.org.au/common/Uploaded%20files/Guidelines/breast-ca-risk-reducing-meds_clinician-guide_22032024.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Pre-treatment checklist:** formal risk assessment (refer to clinical genetics if the family history is concerning), full history including interacting drugs, menopausal status, a normal breast examination, and if age-appropriate a normal mammogram or breast MRI within 12 months.
claims.locator: Clinical Oncology Society of Australia (COSA), 'Medications to lower the risk of breast cancer: clinician guide', Version 7, approved by COSA Council 22 March 2024, https://www.cosa.org.au/common/Uploaded%20files/Guidelines/breast-ca-risk-reducing-meds_clinician-guide_22032024.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Count a woman as post-menopausal only if** she is 60 or older, has had both ovaries removed, is under 60 with a uterus and more than 12 months of unexplained amenorrhoea, or is under 60 without a uterus and has FSH above 30 IU/L.
claims.locator: Clinical Oncology Society of Australia (COSA), 'Medications to lower the risk of breast cancer: clinician guide', Version 7, approved by COSA Council 22 March 2024, https://www.cosa.org.au/common/Uploaded%20files/Guidelines/breast-ca-risk-reducing-meds_clinician-guide_22032024.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Start with a 6-8 week trial**, then review side-effects. A woman who cannot tolerate one option may manage low-dose tamoxifen, or after menopause a different medicine.
claims.locator: Clinical Oncology Society of Australia (COSA), 'Medications to lower the risk of breast cancer: clinician guide', Version 7, approved by COSA Council 22 March 2024, https://www.cosa.org.au/common/Uploaded%20files/Guidelines/breast-ca-risk-reducing-meds_clinician-guide_22032024.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Tamoxifen practicalities:** premenopausal women start on day 1 of a period and use non-hormonal contraception; stop 4-6 weeks before elective surgery; stop at least 3 months before trying to conceive.
claims.locator: Clinical Oncology Society of Australia (COSA), 'Medications to lower the risk of breast cancer: clinician guide', Version 7, approved by COSA Council 22 March 2024, https://www.cosa.org.au/common/Uploaded%20files/Guidelines/breast-ca-risk-reducing-meds_clinician-guide_22032024.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Review at least yearly until treatment stops:** reassess risk (especially after new family genetic results), manage side-effects and bleeding, check contraception and contraindications, arrange yearly imaging if age-appropriate, repeat bone density every 2 years on an aromatase inhibitor, and stop after 5 years at most.
claims.locator: Clinical Oncology Society of Australia (COSA), 'Medications to lower the risk of breast cancer: clinician guide', Version 7, approved by COSA Council 22 March 2024, https://www.cosa.org.au/common/Uploaded%20files/Guidelines/breast-ca-risk-reducing-meds_clinician-guide_22032024.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **PBS and TGA status:** tamoxifen 20 mg is PBS-listed for women with lifetime risk at least 1.5 times the population level. Raloxifene is TGA-approved for high-risk post-menopausal women but has never been put forward for PBS listing, and the aromatase inhibitors are used off-label.
claims.locator: Clinical Oncology Society of Australia (COSA), 'Medications to lower the risk of breast cancer: clinician guide', Version 7, approved by COSA Council 22 March 2024, https://www.cosa.org.au/common/Uploaded%20files/Guidelines/breast-ca-risk-reducing-meds_clinician-guide_22032024.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23
